newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris splits stock, sets $8 billion buyback.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris splits stock, sets $8 billion buyback.

text.p: Food and tobacco giant Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Wednesday announced a three-for-one split of its common stock and a new three-year $8 billion share repurchase programme.

The New York-based consumer goods giant, whose products include Marlboro cigarettes, Miller beer and Kraft foods, also declared an unchanged quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share on the pre-split common stock.

The news prompted several Wall Street firms to repeat recommendations to buy the stock, helping boost the price to a new 12-month high of $136.75. It gave up most of the day's gains, however, ending up 12.5 cents at $133.50 on the New York Stock Exchange, after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned about the sustainability of sharp gains in stock prices.

To effect the split, two additional common shares will be distributed on April 10 for each share held of record as of March 17. Including the latest split, Philip Morris' common stock will have been split seven times since Jan. 1, 1966, with the result that one share in 1966 is now the equivalent of 576 shares, it said.

Philip Morris said its current three-year $6 billion stock repurchase programme, begun in the fourth quarter of 1994, will be completed by the end of March. Under that programme, the company has bought back 66.3 million shares at an average cost of $84.09 per share through Feb. 25, 1997.
Analysts agreed that with Philip Morris shares trading in the $130-range the repurchases will cost more than in the past, but they said they were still a good value.
"It will be additive to per-share earnings immediately," said Emanuel Goldman, analyst at PaineWebber Group Inc.
Goldman said he was keeping a buy rating on Philip Morris because he considered the stock cheap even as it trades near its 12-month high.
John Maxwell, analyst at Wheat First Butcher Singer, said the buyback was a good move because the stock was "bloody cheap." He has an "aggressive buy" rating on Philip Morris.
Martin Feldman, analyst at Smith Barney Inc., said the share price could reach $145 by the end of 1997 and also has an "aggressive buy" rating on it.
He noted that within the past year concerns over tobacco litigation drove the stock price from about $105 to $85, but he said $85 turned out to be a good buying opportunity.

With 1996 revenues of $69 billion, Philip Morris is the world's largest producer and marketer of consumer packaged goods. Its five principal operating companies are Kraft Foods, Inc., Miller Brewing Co., Philip Morris International Inc., Philip Morris U.S.A.and Philip Morris Capital Corp.
